set_title: A study is described: which design is it
stem: Researchers study whether arsenic in well water is linked to bladder cancer. They enroll 120 patients who have bladder cancer and 240 people who do not, then ask every participant about the arsenic level of wells used earlier in life.
oneliner: Arsenic and bladder cancer: 120 patients with it + 240 people without, past well-water exposure asked of both → ?
ask: Which study design is this?

whyNot.A: A cohort study sorts participants by exposure and follows them for new disease; here the groups were chosen by **bladder cancer status**, and exposure was asked about afterward
whyNot.B: A crossover trial gives each participant two treatments in turn; here **no treatment is given** and only past exposure is asked about
whyNot.D: A case series describes patients without a comparison group; here **240 people without bladder cancer** are compared with 120 patients
whyNot.E: A cross-sectional study samples one population and measures exposure and disease together; here **patients and non-patients were enrolled as separate groups**

why: The investigators chose participants by outcome, 120 with bladder cancer and 240 without, and then looked backward for arsenic exposure. **Enrolling by disease status and looking back at exposure** defines a case-control study. It yields an odds ratio, not incidence or prevalence.

stem: A company records solvent exposure when 3000 factory workers are hired and sorts them into an exposed group and an unexposed group. All workers are followed for 10 years, and new cases of leukemia are counted in each group.
oneliner: 3000 factory workers sorted by solvent exposure at hire, followed 10 years for new leukemia → ?

whyNot.C: A randomized trial has the investigators assign the exposure by chance; here the company **records the exposure at hire** and no one is assigned to it

why: Workers were grouped by exposure and followed forward for the outcome, which is a cohort design. **Grouping by exposure and following forward to new disease** allows incidence and relative risk to be calculated, which a case-control study cannot do.

whyNot.C: A case series describes patients without comparing treatments; here **two drugs are compared in the same 30 patients**

stem: Researchers are comparing two cholesterol-lowering drugs for the prevention of myocardial infarction. options.A: Patients are followed forward for 5 years

options.C: A chance process assigns each patient's drug
options.D: Each group is enrolled at the start of follow-up
options.E: New myocardial infarctions are counted in each group

stem: A 62-year-old woman is about to have an operation for a tumor. After this operation, the proportions of patients who survive each successive year are 90% in year 1, 80% in year 2, 75% in year 3 and 60% in year 4. She asks for the chance that she will be alive 4 years after the operation.
oneliner: 62F + about to have surgery + yearly survival 90%, 80%, 75%, 60% + asks chance of being alive at year 4 → ?
ask: Which calculation gives her chance of being alive 4 years after the operation?

whyNot.A: Averaging the four yearly proportions has no meaning for survival; she must survive **year 1, then year 2, then year 3, then year 4**, so the proportions multiply
whyNot.B: This drops the 90% for year 1; **she has not yet survived any year**, so year 1 must be included
whyNot.E: This drops years 1 and 2; **she has only just been operated on**, so nothing has been survived yet
whyNot.D: This is the proportion for year 4 alone, which applies only to **a patient who is already alive at the start of year 4**

why: A patient who has just started follow-up must live through every interval in turn, so the yearly proportions multiply: 0.90 × 0.80 × 0.75 × 0.60 = 0.324. **From time zero, multiply all the intervals up to the time asked.**

set_title: A clinical dilemma: which ethical principle or duty is at stake
stem: A 31-year-old man is unconscious after a fall from a roof. CT shows an expanding intracranial hematoma that will be fatal within the hour without surgery. No relative can be reached and he has no advance directive. The surgeon decides whether to operate.
oneliner: 31M + unconscious with a fatal expanding hematoma + no relative reachable, no advance directive → ?
ask: Which ethical principle should most directly guide the surgeon's decision?

whyNot.C: Autonomy rests on a choice made by the patient or a surrogate; he is unconscious, **no relative can be reached and he has no advance directive**
whyNot.A: Nonmaleficence argues against an intervention that does more harm than good; the hematoma **will be fatal within the hour without surgery**, so operating is the beneficial step
whyNot.E: Justice concerns fair allocation among patients; the stem **describes one patient and no scarce resource**
whyNot.B: Confidentiality concerns disclosure of information; the stem **describes no disclosure**

why: When a patient cannot consent, no surrogate can be found and delay would be fatal, the physician acts under implied consent to protect his life. **Acting for the patient's good in an emergency, with no one able to decide, is beneficence.**

why: The father's exact worry is unknown, and her growth is normal. Reassurance or tests first would miss the real concern. **Start by asking an open-ended question about the concern.**
